The best interface is the one you forget
On calm software, fewer settings and the art of getting out of the way.
We spend an enormous amount of energy making software noticeable. Bigger buttons, brighter badges, more notifications. But the tools people love most are the ones they barely think about.
Think of a good pen. You don't admire the pen while you write. You admire what you wrote. The pen has done its job precisely by disappearing.
Every setting is a question you are asking the user. Sometimes that question is necessary. More often, it's a decision the team didn't want to make.
> The kindest thing a tool can do is decide well on your behalf.
When we removed forty percent of the options from our settings page, support tickets went down, not up. People didn't miss the choices. They missed the friction.
A calm interface respects attention as a limited resource. It waits until it's needed. It speaks softly. It remembers what you did last time.
None of this is new. But it's easy to forget when every metric rewards being seen.
Why the night sky is brighter this winter
A comet, a planet and a very clear stretch of weather walk into a sky.
If you've stepped outside on a clear night recently, you might have noticed more than usual. You're not imagining it.
A comet is making its closest pass in decades. Look low in the west just after sunset, and give your eyes twenty minutes to adjust.
> Binoculars help, but this one you can see with your eyes alone.
Jupiter is also at its brightest, a steady cream-coloured point that doesn't twinkle the way stars do.
A recipe is a story you tell with your hands.
My grandmother cooked by sound and smell. The onions were ready when they whispered. The bread was done when it sounded hollow.
When she was ninety, I tried to write her recipes down. Every answer was a little shrug. 'Enough flour.' 'Until it looks right.'
> Some knowledge only lives in the doing.
I still don't measure the garlic. I think she'd approve.
I rebuilt my side project in a weekend. Here's what broke.
The plan was simple: rewrite the whole thing over a long weekend. The code went fine. Everything around the code did not.
Emails stopped sending. Old links broke. A cron job I'd forgotten about quietly kept running on the old server for three days.
> Rewrites fail at the edges, not in the middle.
Next time I'll write down every invisible job the old system did before I touch anything.
This put words to something I've felt for years.
